title: Testing at the Bedside: Waived Tests, Proficiency Testing and Site Comparisons
summary: Apply US CLIA rules to point-of-care testing: what makes a test system waived, what a certificate of waiver allows, how proficiency samples must be handled, and why bedside and central-lab results must be compared twice a year.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 7 Hits 1 and 3 and Traps 2 and 6 (first lesson for Ch. 7), from the CLIA regulation text (42 CFR 493.15, 493.35, 493.801, 493.1281; eCFR version 2026-10-01). US-only; Philippine rules are not covered. Not taught as fact: the named glucometer (StatStrip) clearance and the 2014 FDA proposal, the waived-laboratory director rule, POCT definition and iatrogenic anaemia, lockouts, operator/lot traceability, hCG assay sensitivity, LIAT and molecular POCT, GAS culture backup, cardiac-marker outcomes, dipstick validation numbers, molecular contamination, POCT1-A2 connectivity, POC creatinine, PT root-cause analysis.

objectives: State the CLIA criteria for waived test systems and what a certificate of waiver allows.
Apply the CLIA rules for handling proficiency-testing samples.
Explain the twice-yearly requirement to compare results across methods, instruments or sites.

scenes.title: Three bedside-testing decisions
scenes.altText: Invented scenario in a US setting: (1) a clinic holding a Certificate of Waiver runs urine dipsticks, visual urine pregnancy tests and a home-use glucose meter, and wants to add an automated CBC analyzer; (2) the hospital hands its POCT glucose proficiency-testing (PT) samples to the laboratory’s most experienced technologist; (3) ward glucose meters and the central-lab glucose method have never been compared. Question token: “Which of these breaks the rules?”

cues.text: A clinic with a certificate of waiver runs dipsticks, pregnancy tests and a home-use glucose meter, and wants to add an automated blood-count analyzer.
The hospital gives its bedside glucose proficiency samples to its most experienced lab technologist. And its ward meters have never been compared with the central lab.
Which of these break the rules for point-of-care testing?

scenes.title: What makes a test “waived”
scenes.altText: Criteria card (42 CFR 493.15(b), US CLIA): waived test systems are simple examinations that (1) are cleared by FDA for home use, (2) use methods so simple and accurate that erroneous results are negligible, or (3) pose no reasonable risk of harm if performed incorrectly. List card (493.15(c)): includes non-automated dipstick urinalysis, non-automated fecal occult blood, visual ovulation and urine-pregnancy tests, non-automated ESR, copper-sulfate haemoglobin, blood glucose by devices FDA-cleared specifically for home use, spun microhaematocrit, and single-analyte haemoglobin instruments; HHS determines additions. Rule card (493.15(e)): waived laboratories must follow the manufacturer’s instructions.

cues.text: In the United States, CLIA defines waived tests as simple examinations: cleared by the FDA for home use, so simple and accurate that errors are negligible, or posing no reasonable risk of harm if done wrong.

The regulation lists examples, such as non-automated urine dipsticks, visual pregnancy tests, spun haematocrit, and blood glucose meters cleared for home use. HHS decides which further tests are added.
Waived status belongs to the specific test system and its clearance, not to the room where it is used.
And a waived laboratory must follow the manufacturer’s instructions exactly.

scenes.title: Certificates, proficiency testing and comparisons
scenes.altText: Certificate card (493.15(c); 493.35): a laboratory qualifies for a CERTIFICATE OF WAIVER only if it restricts testing to waived tests “and no others”; it files an application describing its tests, methods and personnel and must permit announced and unannounced inspections. PT card (493.801(b)): PT samples must be tested with the regular patient workload BY PERSONNEL WHO ROUTINELY PERFORM THE TESTING, using routine methods, the same number of times as patient samples; no inter-laboratory (or inter-site) communication about results before the reporting deadline; never send PT samples to another laboratory. Comparison card (493.1281): if the same test is performed with different methods or instruments, or at multiple sites, the laboratory must evaluate and define the relationship between results TWICE A YEAR, and document it.

cues.text: A certificate of waiver covers waived tests and no others. Adding a non-waived test, such as an automated blood-count analyzer, needs a different certificate and more requirements.
Proficiency samples must be tested like patients: within the normal workload, by the people who routinely do the testing, using routine methods, and the same number of times.
Results must not be discussed with other labs or sites before the deadline, and PT samples must never be sent to another laboratory.
And when the same test runs on different instruments or at several sites, such as ward meters and the central lab, the results must be compared and their relationship documented twice a year.

scenes.title: Applying the rules
scenes.altText: Decision card. (1) Waiver clinic + automated CBC → the certificate of waiver no longer fits, because the clinic would no longer be restricted to waived tests; it needs an appropriate certificate for non-waived testing. (2) PT given to the “best” technologist → violates 493.801(b)(1): PT must be run by personnel who routinely perform the testing, within routine workload. (3) Ward meters never compared → violates 493.1281(a): define the relationship between methods/sites twice a year. Scope card: these are US federal rules (CLIA, 42 CFR 493); other countries (e.g. the Philippines) have their own licensing rules, which this lesson does not cover. Hook answer: all three break the rules.

cues.text: Apply the rules. The waiver clinic cannot just add an automated blood counter: it would no longer be restricted to waived tests, so it needs a certificate that covers non-waived testing.
Handing proficiency samples to the most experienced technologist breaks the rule that the people who routinely test must test them, within the normal workload.
Never comparing ward meters with the central lab breaks the twice-yearly comparison requirement.
So all three break the rules. Remember these are US federal rules; other countries, including the Philippines, have their own requirements.

lines: US CLIA only · local rules differ

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A test becomes waived because it is done at the bedside” (✓ waived status follows the specific test system and its FDA clearance, not the location); “Give PT samples to your best technologist” (✓ PT is run by personnel who routinely perform the testing, within the routine workload); “Discuss a puzzling PT result with a sister lab before submitting” (✓ no inter-laboratory or inter-site communication until after the reporting deadline).

cues.text: Trap one: a test becomes waived because it is done at the bedside. No: waived status follows the specific test system and its clearance.
Trap two: give proficiency samples to your best technologist. No: the people who routinely perform the test must run them, in the normal workload.
Trap three: check a puzzling result with a sister laboratory before submitting. No: no communication about PT results until after the reporting deadline.

scenes.title: Treat PT like a patient
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Treat the PT sample like a PATIENT: same hands, same workload, same method, same number of runs, no phone-a-friend, no referral. And meters on the ward are TWINS of the lab analyzer — check they still match twice a year.” Tokens: waived = system, not room · PT = patient · compare ×2/yr. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: treat the proficiency sample like a patient. Same hands, same workload, same method, same number of runs, no phone-a-friend and no referral. And check that ward meters still match the lab twice a year.
Where it breaks: these are United States federal rules and other countries differ; accrediting bodies may add stricter requirements; and the waived-test list changes as new systems are cleared.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Waived = simple, low-risk test systems (493.15); certificate of waiver = waived tests only; follow manufacturer instructions”, “PT by routine staff in routine workload, no communication/referral (493.801) · compare methods/sites twice a year (493.1281)”.

cues.text: Under US CLIA, waived status belongs to the test system, a certificate of waiver covers waived tests only, proficiency samples must be tested like patients by routine staff without communication or referral, and results across methods or sites must be compared twice a year.

props.label: Waived = test system · waiver certificate = waived only · follow insert
PT = like a patient, no talk/referral · compare sites ×2/year

explanation.what: Plain language: in the US, very simple, low-risk tests can be run under a light “waiver” licence, but only those tests; quality checks with outside samples must be done exactly like real patient testing; and bedside meters must be checked against the main lab regularly. Scientific terms: CLIA, waived test system, certificate of waiver, manufacturer’s instructions, proficiency testing (PT), inter-laboratory communication, PT referral, comparison of test results.
explanation.why: Waiver rests on the test system’s simplicity and low risk, so it is tied to the cleared device and its instructions. PT only measures real performance if samples are handled like patient specimens. Different methods or sites can drift apart, so their relationship must be re-defined regularly.
explanation.measure: Waived criteria and list (493.15); certificate of waiver: waived tests only, inspections (493.15(c), 493.35); PT: routine personnel, routine workload and methods, same number of runs, no communication before deadline, no referral (493.801(b)); method/site comparison twice a year, documented (493.1281).
explanation.differs: Waived vs non-waived (moderate/high complexity) testing; PT handled like patient samples vs special handling (prohibited); single-method lab vs multi-site/multi-method (comparison required).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: decide whether a site can stay under a certificate of waiver, identify PT handling violations, and recognize the twice-yearly comparison rule for POCT devices.

questions.stem: A US clinic holds a certificate of waiver and wants to add a test that is not on the waived list. What is required?

options.text: A certificate appropriate for non-waived testing, because a waiver covers waived tests only
options.rationale: Correct. 493.15(c): the laboratory must restrict testing to waived tests “and no others”.

options.text: Nothing, if the test is done at the bedside
options.rationale: Incorrect. Location does not change categorization.

options.text: Only a note in the procedure manual
options.rationale: Incorrect. The certificate type must change.

options.text: Running the test only on weekends

questions.stem: Which practice complies with CLIA proficiency-testing rules?

options.text: Testing PT samples within the routine workload by staff who routinely perform the test
Running PT samples in triplicate when patients are run once
options.rationale: Incorrect. PT must be tested the same number of times as patients.

options.text: Sending a PT sample to a reference lab to confirm
Comparing PT results with another site before the deadline
options.rationale: Incorrect. No inter-site communication before the deadline.

questions.stem: A hospital measures glucose with ward meters and with a central-laboratory analyzer. How often must it evaluate the relationship between their results?

options.text: Only when a new meter is purchased
options.rationale: Incorrect. The requirement is ongoing, twice a year.
Incorrect. Clearance does not remove the comparison requirement.
